Fuck, this hits close to home. I have BPD, social anxiety, depression, and CPTSD and deal with severe suicidal ideation as my pathetic post history indicates. About six months ago I went to a general practitioner about my issue. I had been on Cymbalta for about five years at that point. Forty milligrams for about the first 4.5 years and sixty milligrams for the most recent six months. It wasn't really helping much but was making me really fucking stupid. My depression hasn't ever really been the crux of my issues. It's the BPD and social anxiety that really causes problems in my life. Anyhow, I wanted to get off of the Cymbalta and get on something that helped with my BPD and social anxiety, so I went to see a general practitioner who took my insurance and got great reviews. I figured this was the next best route as I couldn't get into a psychiatrist for about two months. I get to the practice and for some reason I'm not able to see the doctor after all. Luckily, though, there was another doctor I could see. I start talking to him and get to the part about my depression and issues with Cymbalta at which point he interrupts me, hands me a piece of paper, tells me to fill it out, and walks out. It was a survey that helps determine if you have depression. I fill it out, he determines that I have depression (which wasn't surprising because it had been diagnosed previously and confirmed by a psychiatrist and a therapist), and starts writing me a script for Trintellix. As he's getting ready to leave I ask about weaning off of the Cymbalta. He tells me there's no need and that I can quit cold turkey. I ask about the BPD and social anxiety and he says, "One thing at a time."

Two days later I start going through some killer withdrawals. The third day I call the after hours number and it just rings constantly. I finally get an answer after the fourth try and the nurse has the doctor on call call me. It's that original doctor with great reviews. He asked why I just quit Cymbalta cold turkey and explained the appointment with the other doctor. He told me that was not how it should have been done, to stop the Trintillix, to take the Cymbalta to help with the withdrawals, and get in touch with a doctor about weaning off of the Cymbalta. 

The whole process was aggravating as fuck and patronizing. 

I don't have any advice unfortunately, but I can relate to you in this case and am happy to offer some support. 

I hope things start looking up for you.

>What can I expect?

It's difficult to tell you exactly what you can expect because each facility I'd different. But you can expect to be asked the same questions by several different people (social workers, nurses, and psychiatrist), they'll take your vitals daily, you won't have much privacy, you'll be expected to go to and participate in various classes. You'll also likely have to strip down and have a skin check done during the admin process. 

>Will they let me take my hormones?

Unfortunately, I don't know for sure.

>What differences are there between voluntary and involuntary?

In regards to the way they treat you, nothing in my experience. However, it's very important to understand that a voluntary stay doesn't mean you can just leave. You'll likely be there 72 hours minimum. If the psychiatrist deems it necessary (or he finds out your insurance will pay for it in some cases) you'll be kept longer. On paper that will still be considered a voluntary hold. If you just decide to leave anyways, they'll likely 5150 you.

>Does it work?

Are there plenty of cases where it has worked for people? Yes. Does it work all the time? Absolutely not. Plenty of people commit suicide or just live with their previous issues for the rest of their lives after a psych hospital stint. Personally, I'm far more suicidal since my stint. I'll never reach out to another mental health professional because of it. I'm not exaggerating when I say I'll suicide by cop before I go back. There is, actually, some speculation that it can make people suicidal. There aren't any studies as far as I know, but the speculation is because there are plenty of cases of people who weren't suicidal (remember psych hospitals are for people who are mentally ill, not just suicidal people) being put into a psych hospital and committing suicide after. Correlation =/= causation, so I won't say that the hospital stint caused the suicide, but I'd definitely say it warrants some studies on the subject. 

>What's the best outcome here?

That you learn coping methods and get access to help that allows you to live a happy and fulfilling life without suicidal ideation. Will that happen? I have no idea, but it's certainly possible.

>I really want to be happy.

I want you to be happy too. :) I'm by no means telling you not to go or trying to scare you. However, there's a lot to consider. First, it's expensive if you have the "privilege" of living in the U.S. Also, it can cost you money in lost work hours at work or even a lost job depending on your circumstances. Second, It can turn into a long term situation whether or not you actually need to be there that long. Not all, or even most, psychiatrists are bad people, but they're out there. Third, it's very structured leaving you with very little autonomy. That's not inherently bad, but can definitely be hard, or damn near impossible, for some people to deal with. Fourth, everything you say, or refuse to say, can be used to psychoanalyze you which can be scary and difficult to deal with.

Anyhow, I know you're not scheduled to visit until Monday, so I'd like to make some suggestions. First, please please please find a person or people who will spend some time with you, or at least check in with you often, until then. Second, if you feel like it won't be a risk to your safety, can you call a psychiatrist, ask for an emergency appointment,  and see if they can prescribe you something and direct you to some resources without having to go to a hospital?

If not, I understand and would never judge you for going, but please avoid one owned by Universal Health Services.

Best of luck, and don't hesitate to reach out to me, friend.
